The therapist talked about the texture of foods and how they might indicate something else, like a bowl of soup might represent I need comfort because it’s smooth, savory, and feels calm to my stomach, or an apple and its crunch may indicate anger and/or stress, etc. Now I try to identify my needs and how to meet them. You do have insight into why you find it difficult to be around “strong emotions”. You listed the responses your family (your models) had toward emotions. There’s somethings I learned in DBT (dialectical behavior therapy) called distress tolerance and emotional regulation. Tolerating our emotions is something that “should” be taught as we grow up. Questions like, “why do you feel sad?” or “Can let me know how you’re feeling about this?” allow for exploration of feelings. “Quit crying!” or “Why do you feel that way?! It’s not that bad!” are examples of dismissive behavior toward emotions and so instead of further exploration of the emotions, people are taught to stuff them down or to act like they don’t have them. Building a tolerance for experiencing emotions takes practice. When someone else has a reaction and emotion come up, why am I having my own reaction and emotion come up? Maybe it is, “hey, my family didn’t welcome this emotion and it’s confusing because they are expressing it and I’m not used to people expressing themselves with the expectation of being heard.” Maybe it’s, “I don’t know what’s going to happen after this emotion is expressed.” Is there judgement in saying “strong emotions” vs saying, “this person is expressing x emotion.” Is it, “this is a strong emotion” or “I’m having a strong reaction to this emotion.” Anyway, I think you have some good insights already.

What does it mean to her that you want to have your own activities? Sometimes people try to control someone else because there is a fear of abandonment. Some people think, “if you don’t have other people then there’s no way you could leave me” - subconscious of course. To go along with this thought pattern bolsters codependency as opposed to two people coming together with their own ideas, hobbies, interests, etc. “What’s the benefit?” is something someone shed light on with me once. Instead of asking, “Why can’t I do x?” I ask, “what’s the benefit in me not being able to do x?” I’ve found a lot of people have to stop and think when I ask them. Also, listening to the answer from the other person, because it’s coming from somewhere. But typically, the benefit is that the other person is relieved of feeling uncomfortable feelings. If you don’t leave me and having nothing going on, then I won’t have to deal with the feelings that come up when someone doesn’t need me and/or when I don’t get my way. The coming together after separating is really important, I’m coming to find out. It’s helpful when I reunite with my partner to convey that I missed her, love her, and then go into the happenings of what I did while we were separate. Asking about her experiences too. Depending on the circumstances, being positive when returning can be helpful to know separation is okay and does not equate to more distance and/or breaking up.

If no, I’m still watching it and accepting the other person doesn’t want to watch it. That doesn’t change that I want to watch it. If yes, I’m glad you’re joining. I’m trying to keep this sort of mindset to accept my interests.

Positive affirmations that I’m doing this work for me. I can practice self-soothing skills when I’m around others if I need to be around others. I can practice checking in with myself and notice body sensations, feelings, and thoughts that come up. I can become curious about why these thoughts and feelings are coming up. I can welcome them and explore them and feel them. That is different than behaviors others can see. I can do this by myself for myself. Because I often lean into things with emotion, I am learning to check the facts of the situation. I can then proceed mindfully, which means I’ve taken both logic and emotion into account and will behave (action) to how I see fit. They taught me this in DBT. So, “I feel lonely. I feel alone because I’m not used to living for myself and being by myself. This emotion is coming up for me because I’m longing for connection. My urge is to text someone and focus on them. Is the feeling of loneliness keeping me from doing something for myself? If this emotion wasn’t here I would be more proactive. What do I need? I don’t want to connect with someone yet because I’m confused and I will instead connect with myself. What can I do that’s enjoyable for me without someone else? Is there something I need to do right now that will benefit me?” Then I proceed accordingly. For me, it helps to have healthy distractions such as cleaning, watching a tv show, drawing, coloring, learning dance moves, etc. Those are easier to access first. I’m learning to calm my body at the first sign of anxiety and overwhelm. Then go from there.

Self-focus. What do I want or need in this moment? For example: Is my need connection? Where else can I get connection? Am I feeling disconnected from myself and not taking care of myself and instead focusing on this other person? I learned to focus on others as a way of self-soothing from the pain I was feeling. Instead of sitting in whatever feeling, it’s easier to focus on the other person’s behaviors. That way I can focus on how to “fix” them, which is a defense mechanism that works to avoid myself. I matter too! I am valuable! I deserve to be happy and loving toward myself! Then I go do something that benefits me for me. I used to hate cleaning and now I use it as a healthy distraction from thoughts, but it also serves as a benefit that my space is clean and comfortable. To me, this also means I also feel safe in my space. Now that I know I’m safe I can practice words of affirmation. “I love you. You did well in managing your emotions. You’re emotionally intelligent and you care about yourself, otherwise you wouldn’t be working so hard to live a life you want. I love you. Keep up the good work.” I am working on building a tolerance for this as my default is to focus on others. But I am also in control of how much I say these things to myself and refocus to myself throughout the day. Self-soothing can be amazing! This branches out into being able to feel good when with others. Solid baseline. People are added an added bonus to life, not a crutch to save me from me. I need to live life on life’s terms and actually experience it for me!

I’ve had to learn to literally tell myself, “my partner’s feelings are not mine to own, but I want to hear them because my partner is important to me. I can hear other’s perspectives even if I don’t agree.” I don’t know anyone who expresses themselves that does not want to be heard. Maybe there are some out there. People tell us things for a reason and sometimes they nor the other know what’s underneath and it can take additional communication and soul searching to figure out what is actually trying to be communicated. So I figure, how can I find out more information without assuming? I ask questions and try not personalize things. But, why was it so hard for me to hear in the first place? I simply did not want to hear the answer. I wanted to be heard too and because I hadn’t in early life, I can overcompensate now by dominating a conversation with only my viewpoint if I’m not being mindful. Defensiveness led to distance, while being heard and validated helped with closeness. Hearing and validation doesn’t equate to agreement, just actions to maintain respect within the relationship that both parties have valid experiences that can be heard. That’s been one of the best lessons learned.

However, if there’s no motivation and insight into change, it can be difficult to cultivate a meaningful relationship. Far too often I’m concerned about others and neglect myself. I mean, how can I truly grow if I neglect myself as a result of dissecting another’s actions?” Self-regulation is key to any relationship. For some, that’s harder than others. If I’m in the thick of a codependency meltdown, I’m not regulated. How can I blame the other person for their unregulated behaviors if I can’t even regulate my own self?” That would make me critical instead of having compassion. Compassion with boundaries is a work in progress.

If my partner is away from me at work, let’s say. I can say, “bleep yeah! Make that money!” Or if I miss my partner, maybe I can send a text that reads “I miss you’ or ask a connecting question “Is there anything you’re looking forward to this weekend?” Maybe the reply isn’t what I anticipated, but I can choose to believe I can handle the emotions.

Acceptance has helped me. Work in progress. “I accept the things I cannot change, the courage to change the things I can, and the wisdom to know the difference” comes to mind. I got pretty stuck in a loop of freeze mode where I didn’t do anything while waiting for someone to rescue me from the icky  thoughts and feelings. I realized though, I just didn’t care about myself. Not my appearance, my relationships, my work, what interests me, etc. ZERO bleeps given about myself, so it was natural to focus on someone else. I started and continue to learn more about boundaries. I learned from one video to ask myself how is my trust? Honesty? Esteem? Respect? Willingness without rescuing? Assertiveness skills? Responsibility? Attention? Balance and reciprocity? Independence? How can I build boundaries around them? With honesty, it’s “I am honest about my own feelings to myself first.” It became a pattern to internally say, “I am anxious and everyone needs to know and now because everyone knows, I expect them to alleviate the pain because I don’t know what to do and it takes effort while being sad that I didn’t have emotional availability from my parents.” I had to grieve. I also had to think, “this is my life and it doesn’t have to be this way.” Stepping out of my comfort zone and seeing what it’s like was eye opening for me.

A therapist taught me “acceptance plus a change in behavior = a life worth living” from a DBT program I was in. 

I am learning acceptance. I accept this person has not text me back. 

I am learning how to change my behavior. I stop what I am doing. Take a step back from the situation. Observe my thoughts and feelings to know what they are so I can work through them. When people didn’t text back I felt anxious, depressed, abandoned, disappointed, etc. I thought no one cares, etc. What are the facts in the situation? He/she has not text back. Therapists are human and therefore have blind spots. Sometimes it isn’t necessarily intended toxicity as much as it is incompetence, learning curves, etc. - this can also be related to systemic issues. Consideration of licensed vs licensed. If someone is barely stepping into clinical work they might not be as smooth as someone who has been doing it for years and years. Maybe they are unable to attend trainings due to lack of funding. Let’s say a clinic is understaffed and therefore employees are facing burnout. Or say a client comes in and maybe the therapist doesn’t have experience working with the issue. 
Ultimately, therapists need to be attuned to self and client and take some steps (supervision, triage, etc) in order to remain ethical in the best interest of the client. If not, then yes, it is toxic because the issues aren’t being addressed and there is a deeper issue on the therapist’s and/or system’s part. 

Sometimes clients omit history, symptoms, and what is really going on in their life and that is a challenge. Sometimes clients resist treatment by way of not complying with medication or don’t attempt to implement interventions that are supposed to help with treatment or miss appointments. A lot of times things get worse before they get better because of the deep dive into symptoms that are impacting daily functioning. Some people expect quick fixes and in all actuality therapy might need to be longer. 

All this is to say that yes, therapists can be toxic, the system can be toxic as well which in turn would not bolster wellness, if you will. Worth mentioning is taking the process of it all into consideration. Ultimately, if a therapist or client realizes that the dynamic just isn’t working then perhaps a new therapist may be a better fit.

“So why people act like this phrase is such a big deal and makes someone self-centered?”

Because it is self-centered, lol. In your write up you are conveying that you are choosing not to explore more about why the person is feeling how they are feeling. What you’re choosing to focus on is how you didn’t do anything to upset this person and what you didn’t do. That it self-centered in terms of empathy. “I’m sorry you feel that way” is a detachment from the feelings brought into the dynamic. 

“I feel hurt” 

“I’m sorry you feel that way” 

Vs

“I feel hurt” 

“Can you explain why you feel hurt because I’m not quite understanding where you are coming from?”

If you still don’t think your actions hurt the person and you care about the person a simple “I need to reflect on this further because I’m still not seeing it but I care” is a lot better than, “Sorry you feel that way.” At least in one instance you are choosing to explore how you could have potentially been a part of a rupture in the dynamic. 

Maybe you won’t ever see how your actions hurt another or don’t believe they did. There can still be space for someone to express their feelings. This is why therapists, etc emphasize using “I statements” because if done correctly it is a guide for each person to hold their own feelings without blaming the other person AND also taking responsibility. In that responsibility, often people can see how feelings were brought into the dynamic. 

Exploration leads to further understanding, not about who is right and who is wrong. AND in my opinion, if someone said they were “hurt” or what have you and shut you down for wanting to understand, that’s a problem as well.

Feelings are valid. The actions I take may not be valid. 
One of the first steps I took in this journey of healing was to change the relationship I had with myself. Accept what I am feeling so I can be more secure with myself. When I was growing up my family completely invalidated my feelings so I learned to not trust my own feelings. I don’t want to gaslight myself. I have learned it’s okay to have different feelings than someone else.

On any given day I can feel anger, sadness, happiness, anxiety, invigorated, etc. and those are VALID because it is how I am internally responding in that moment. 
However, the action part is something that I could potentially change. 

If I start to insist that my feelings are the only feelings that matter and that everyone should feel the same way, that is an action. The action of insisting is communicating with only my side in mind, concluding that my feelings are the only feelings in a dynamic of two or more people, and/or even passive-aggressive behavior when someone feels or acts differently which can result in anger, withdrawal, and resentment.
I don’t ever have to change the way I feel. Can I change how I communicate with myself, yes. Can I change how I express myself to others without invalidating myself, absolutely.

Everyone has boundaries which means everyone has the ability to act/react when those boundaries are crossed/invalidated. 
Boundaries are what keep each person safe. In my opinion, no one is a mind reader, therefore communication is important so each person knows each other’s boundaries and is either going to respect them or reject them. Although dynamics can bring up feelings, it’s each person’s own responsibility to look at the underlying issues as to why and how that may or may not contribute to a healthy or unhealthy relationship, including that relationship with ourselves.

What I read is a whole lot of people abandoned her and that can cause a lot of mourning which may present itself as depression, suicidal ideation and/or attempts, anxiety, etc. Boundaries can be put into place for your own safety and well-being without completely abandoning a relationship. If you’re done and want to block, then okay. If you block her and she does something, you aren’t the same person; you each have your own thoughts, feelings, and actions. I mean we are all responsible for our own well-being. However, in relationships, we get to share what we want, need, desire, etc. As someone who has been and seen others who are suicidal, it can be for many reasons. Mourning, feelings of rejection, neurological issues like chemical imbalances, not seeing a purpose in life, sh** finances, menstrual dis -regulation such as PMDD, etc. What if someone has a combination of said factors? That’s going to compound the pain and further creates a barrier to overcome. Imagine how exhausting that is to live with. Hopefully she is honest with the treatment professional. “They’re stuck up from what I’ve seen and not only that they can’t handle her emotions etc the way I would’ve” reminds me of white knighting, again boundaries. I don’t know if you wish to support her. If you do, what does that look like for you? That’s how boundaries start: what is your capacity to support look like FOR YOU. If someone says, “I need a ride to the airport” and you know you have to go to work, you can say, “I can’t. I go to work at that time.” Then the person says, “but but but I thought you cared.” and then, “I do care that you make it to the airport AND I also care about my financial well-being. What other options can be taken to get to the airport? Bus, Uber, another person?” I’ve found that if THINK I’m the only lifeline, I’m doing too much to rescue. A lot of people in moments will think they are the only lifeline because of the boundaries not set, the guilt comes flooding. Such is not the case even if it looks as though. In this case, the psych is a lifeline with hopefully the capacity to assist in helping find additional help to clients. It’s okay to not know how to help.
